opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the thing that cellular automata get right, and that a lot of our standard models of computation get wrong, or at least abstract away, is that computation is always happening *somewhere*. It's happening in a physical medium, with locality, where things can only affect their neighbors, and where the machine doing the computing is made out of the same stuff as the data it's computing on.

When Turing wrote down his machine, there's this very clean separation: you've got the head, you've got the tape, the head reads and writes the tape, but the head itself is sort of outside the world. It's not on the tape. And that's a great abstraction for proving things about computability, but it's not how life works, and it's not how any real computer works either. A real computer is made of atoms, it can be damaged, it can be rewritten. A cell is a chemical system that is computing and also building itself out of the products of its computation.

Von Neumann understood this really deeply. That's why, when he started thinking about self-reproduction, he didn't do it with a Turing machine in the abstract. He went to a cellular automaton, at Ulam's suggestion, because he wanted a universe where the constructor itself is embedded in the grid. The machine that builds a copy of itself has to be made of cells in the same space it's operating on. And what he figured out, before Watson and Crick, is that to do that you need something like a tape, an instruction description, that gets both interpreted and copied. That is essentially the logic of DNA and ribosomes. So in a sense, the cellular automaton framing let him discover the architecture of life from first principles.

And this connects to some of the work we've been doing with what we've called BFF, these soups of little programs in a minimal language, where the programs and the data are the same thing. You start with random noise, nothing designed, and the programs interact with each other, and they can modify each other. And after a while, quite suddenly, you get a phase transition where self-replicators emerge spontaneously. Nobody put them there. And once you have replication, you get selection, you get increasing complexity, you get symbiosis, programs fusing with other programs.

The reason that works is precisely because it's embodied in this sense: there's no privileged outside interpreter. Everything that's computing can be computed upon. And I think that's the key ingredient for the emergence of life, and frankly for understanding intelligence too. Intelligence isn't some abstract function floating free of the world; it's something that arises in systems that have to maintain and reproduce themselves, that are made of the same stuff they're acting on. Cellular automata are the simplest place you can see that clearly. They strip away everything except locality, uniform rules, and the fact that the computer is part of the world. And it turns out that's enough to get you an astonishing amount.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the Turing machine’s head and tape, explaining that the head manipulates the tape but sits outside the world of symbols.

r003.rationale: It says the embedded machine builds a copy of itself within the cellular automaton.

r004.rationale: It describes computation in a physical medium and mentions atoms, but does not characterize memory as being read and written in atoms rather than abstract bits.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that's so appealing about cellular automata is that they strip computation down to something that is really physical. There's no central processor, there's no global clock in the sense of something sitting outside the system orchestrating it, there's no separation between the program and the thing the program is acting on. You've just got a grid of cells, each one can only see its immediate neighbors, each one updates according to a very simple local rule, and that's it. And yet out of that you can get universality. The Game of Life can compute anything a Turing machine can compute. So you've got this existence proof that computation doesn't require any of the architectural scaffolding we normally associate with it. It can just arise from locality and simple rules.

And that matters for thinking about embodiment because that's what biology is. Your cells don't have access to a global state. A cell in your liver doesn't know what's happening in your foot. It only knows what its neighbors are doing, what chemicals are diffusing through, what signals it's receiving across the membrane. And somehow, out of that purely local interaction, you get an organism that develops from a single cell, that maintains itself, that regenerates when it's damaged. Development, morphogenesis, these are computations that are being done without a computer in the traditional sense. The computation is the physics, or it's the chemistry. It's distributed through the substance of the thing.

So when we started working on neural cellular automata, the idea was to take that same kind of local update rule but make it learnable, so that instead of hand-crafting the rule, you train it with gradient descent. And what you find is that you can get these systems to grow a target pattern from a single seed, and crucially, they'll regenerate it if you cut a piece out. Nobody told the system how to regenerate. That robustness just falls out of the fact that the rule is local and the process is ongoing, that the thing is never "done," it's continuously maintaining itself. Which is very different from how we normally build software, where you compute an answer and then you stop.

The other thing I'd say is that it changes how you think about what intelligence or life even is. If you take the view that computation is fundamental, that it's the substrate out of which these phenomena emerge, then you want the most minimal model of computation that still captures the relevant features, and I think cellular automata are that. They let you ask questions like, how does complexity arise? How do symbiotic structures form? How do you get from randomness to something that replicates and persists? We've done experiments where you just start with random programs in a soup, and self-replicators emerge spontaneously, and then they start to interact and build on each other. That's a very different picture of computation than the one most of us were trained on, where computation is a thing you do to data. Here it's more like computation is a thing that happens, that grows, that's embedded in a space and has to contend with its neighbors. And I think that's much closer to what brains and bodies are actually doing.

r002.rationale: It says cellular automata lack a separation between program and what it acts on, but does not identify the Turing-machine distinction between manipulated symbols and the machinery manipulating them.

r003.rationale: It mentions self-replicators emerging in a soup, but does not state that a machine implemented within a cellular automaton constructs another instance of itself.

r004.rationale: It describes computation as distributed through physical substance, but does not characterize embodied computation in terms of memory read and written in atoms rather than abstract bits.

astra-6.text:
Well, a cellular automaton gives us a very simple way to think about computation as something that happens in space and time. You have a collection of cells, each with some state, and each updates according to what’s happening in its local neighborhood. There’s no central processor looking at the whole thing. And yet those local interactions can produce extraordinarily rich behavior.

That’s useful because physical computation has that character too. A brain isn’t an abstract program floating free of matter. It’s a physical system whose parts interact, where communication takes time and the arrangement of those parts matters. Cellular automata let us explore those constraints in a setting where the underlying rules can be very simple.

You can also get persistent patterns that move around and interact. Those patterns aren’t separate from the medium; they’re things the medium is doing. I think that’s a useful starting point for thinking about an embodied agent: how can a process maintain itself, respond to its surroundings, and act within the same world that constitutes it?

So the appeal isn’t that cellular automata are necessarily a literal model of brains or of physics. It’s that they help us ask how computation, organization, and perhaps agency can emerge from local physical interactions, rather than assuming a computer and its inputs and outputs from the outset.

r002.rationale: It contrasts physical systems with abstract programs, but does not identify a separation in the Turing-machine model between manipulated symbols and the machinery manipulating them.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a cellular automaton gives you a very simple way to think about computation as something that happens in space. You have cells, each with some state, and each cell updates according to what’s happening in its neighborhood. There’s no central processor looking at the whole thing. And yet those local interactions can produce surprisingly rich behavior.

That’s useful for thinking about embodiment because, in a physical system, information has to travel. Things have locations; interactions take time. You don’t get to assume that any part of the system can instantly read or change any other part. Cellular automata make those constraints part of the computational model from the beginning.

And they let you see how something we might call an object—or even a little machine—can itself be a persistent pattern of activity. The distinction between the computer and what it’s computing becomes less obvious. I think that’s a productive starting point for understanding living systems: computation isn’t just an abstract description imposed on the physical process. It’s something the process is doing through its own local interactions.
